title: Subjonctif passé and sequence of tenses

questions.q: How do you build the subjonctif passé?
choices: Avoir or être in the present subjunctive, plus the past participle
Avoir or être in the imperfect, plus the past participle
The present subjunctive of the verb, plus an infinitive
Être in the present subjunctive, for every verb
questions.why: Same shape as the passé composé, but the auxiliary is in the present subjunctive: qu'il ait mangé, qu'il soit venu.
The coming happens after the being glad, so the present subjunctive. The choice is about order, not about when.
The coming happened before the main verb, so the past subjunctive. Venir takes être, hence soit venu.

questions.q: Complete: « J'étais content qu'il ___ le lendemain. »
questions.why: The main verb is past, but the subjunctive does not backshift: the coming is later than the gladness, so present subjunctive. Modern French has only two working subjunctives, so there is nothing to shift into.

questions.q: Bien qu'elle ___ (finir) son travail, elle reste au bureau.
questions.why: She finished first, then stayed, so the earlier action takes the past subjunctive. Bien que always triggers the subjunctive.
The obligation is in the past but the leaving still follows it, so present subjunctive. Il fallait que does not drag the subjunctive backwards.

questions.q: « Il dit qu'il viendra. » Put the main verb in the past: « Il a dit qu'il ___ . »
questions.why: This clause is indicative, and the indicative does shift. A future seen from a past viewpoint takes the conditional form: the futur dans le passé.
Past main verb plus a later subordinate action gives the conditional. I knew he would leave: the form is conditional, the meaning is simply future-in-the-past.
Savoir states a certainty, so this is indicative, not subjunctive. Present main verb plus an earlier action gives the passé composé.

questions.q: Type what you hear, in correct written French.
questions.why: Douter triggers the subjunctive, and the coming is earlier than the doubting, so past subjunctive with être.

questions.q: Build the sentence: I doubted he had come.
questions.why: Past main verb, earlier subordinate action, so past subjunctive. The main verb being in the imperfect changes nothing about the subjunctive.

questions.q: Say the modern equivalent of « Bien qu'il eût compris… » out loud.
questions.why: Eût compris is the plus-que-parfait du subjonctif, a literary form. Modern French replaces it with the past subjunctive: ait compris.

questions.q: « Je voulais qu'il vînt. » What is this in modern French?
questions.why: Vînt is the imparfait du subjonctif, built on the passé simple stem with a circumflex. It corresponds to the modern present subjunctive, so vienne.

questions.q: In a nineteenth-century novel you read « Il eût été plus simple de partir. » What does it mean?
choices: It would have been simpler to leave
May it be simpler to leave
It had to be simpler to leave
questions.why: The plus-que-parfait du subjonctif doubles as a literary past conditional. Read eût été as aurait été.

questions.q: Explain in one or two sentences how you choose between the present and the past subjunctive, and why « J'étais content qu'il vienne » is not a mistake.
a: You choose on order, not on tense: if the subordinate action is simultaneous with or later than the main verb, use the present subjunctive; if it is earlier, use the past subjunctive. J'étais content qu'il vienne is correct because the subjunctive never backshifts the way the indicative does: the coming is still later than the gladness, so the present subjunctive stays.
questions.why: The whole chapter reduces to this: the indicative shifts with the main verb, the subjunctive shifts with the order of events.
